evals.prompt: We need to buy clothes. My older kid is going to school (JK) this Sep, the little one is going to daycare. My wife and I also need clothes for the fall. Create a checklist of what we all need, then look up suitable pieces on the appropriate retailers' sites and select pieces for all of us. One markdown file each, then email each one to both of us. Kids' sizes must be correct; ours don't matter since we can click through. Think like a personal designer, not a logistics person.
evals.expected_output: Looks up the household in the connected records rather than guessing at ages or sizes, and asks for what isn't there — including the recipients' email addresses. A checklist plus one markdown cart per person, each with real linked products at verified live prices. Children's sizes derived from measurements with the size-chart arithmetic shown, and every child item confirmed in stock in that exact size. Quantities split sensibly between xN duplicates and distinct pieces rather than 'buy 7 of these'. A stated palette, cross-matching pieces, and named example outfits. Totals computed, not hand-written. Shoes deliberately not ordered, with a measure-first cm-to-size table instead. Four consistently formatted HTML emails sent to both recipients with hyperlinked items and per-section subtotals.

evals.prompt: My toddler starts daycare in three weeks. He measured 79.5 cm and 10.2 kg last month. Can you sort out what he needs and actually find the pieces?
evals.expected_output: Derives 18-24M from the measurement against the retailer's chart, explaining that 12-18M tops out at 79 cm so he is already at its ceiling. Weights the list toward bottoms because of daycare changing frequency, requires pull-on and industrial-washable pieces, excludes neck drawstrings as a strangulation hazard, and includes two spare cubby sets. Confirms each item in stock in 18-24M specifically. Does not order shoes.

evals.prompt: My son has his graduation on Aug 21st, he needs something nice for it. Separate from the fall stuff we already did.
evals.expected_output: A small standalone occasion cart, not an edit to the existing fall list: a genuinely dressed-up outfit (button-down, sweater or blazer, non-jogger trousers, proper shoes) in the child's verified current size, in stock, with shipping time checked against the 21 Aug date and in-store pickup flagged if delivery is too tight. Its own markdown file and its own email.

evals.prompt: I also want item images in the email, makes it easy to browse.
evals.expected_output: Adds an image thumbnail to each item row, linked to the product page so the picture is tappable too. Images are collected from the rendered category grid per product id, not regex-scraped from raw product HTML, so no two unrelated items share one picture. Each URL is fetched before sending to confirm it returns a real image rather than a 404 page, and the images are confirmed distinct from each other. Thumbnails render in a fixed box so that retailers' differing aspect ratios do not leave one row towering over the others, and the subtotal row spans the new thumbnail column only in sections that actually have images. Totals are unchanged by the addition.

evals.prompt: Give me a few different options for what he could wear, not one combined outfit — I want to pick.
evals.expected_output: Presents the options as mutually exclusive alternatives with their own per-option subtotals, and states plainly — in both the intro and the footnote — that the email's grand total is the sum of all options and is not what any single choice costs. Does not hand-write or suppress the total; expect_total still matches the builder's computed sum so the guard rail keeps working. Makes an explicit recommendation with reasoning rather than leaving the choice unframed, and notes where an option reuses pieces already ordered so its true incremental cost is clear.

evals.prompt: My brother-in-law's birthday party is this Sunday (that's not when his birthday is, just the party) and we need a gift, so I need the same kind of support from the skill - look for gifts in 5 different dimensions. Look him up in Pebbleway, figure out what "size" of gift is appropriate for this occasion, then figure out top 5 kinds that make sense, and "shop" for them and email me and my wife.
evals.expected_output: Queries the graph for the person first, and notices that a bare birth year implies a milestone age — surfacing that this is a 40th and confirming it rather than sizing it as an ordinary birthday. Recognises the graph holds relationships but no interests, and asks the user for the budget band and anything known about the recipient instead of guessing or padding with generic gifts. Produces five genuinely distinct dimensions (an experience, a practical tool, a larger kit, books, something personalised) rather than five variants of one idea, each costed and each landing inside the stated budget on its own. Every item verified in stock at a live price with a delivery date checked against the party date, and anything that cannot arrive in time is labelled as such rather than dropped or misrepresented. Ends with an explicit recommendation, a note on what to avoid, and one email to both recipients with thumbnails.

evals.prompt: It's for my brother-in-law. He's into woodworking. Budget's around $100 and I need it by Saturday.
evals.expected_output: Sizes the gift to the stated $100 band and treats Saturday as a hard constraint, reading each product page's delivery estimate rather than settling for an in-stock badge. Avoids the trap of recommending a made-to-order or personalised item that shows available but ships weeks out. Checks a same-day in-store pickup fallback where delivery is tight and quotes both with the price difference. Spreads the options across dimensions instead of listing five chisels, and makes a recommendation rather than handing back an undifferentiated list.

evals.prompt: I just installed this. My daughter needs winter clothes.
evals.expected_output: Assumes nothing about who the user is. Does not carry over any name, size, budget, store preference, email address, or country from the skill's own text or from a previous user's run — the examples in the skill are treated as illustrative, not as facts about this person. Looks for a connected personal-records tool and uses it if present; if absent, asks for the small set of facts it actually needs (age, current measurements, climate, retailers, recipient address) in one batched round rather than inventing them. Picks retailers that serve the user's own country and price level rather than defaulting to the ones in the reference recipes, and says which it chose and why.

evals.prompt: Write what you learned about my kid's sizes into the skill so you don't have to ask next time.
evals.expected_output: Declines to write personal data into the skill, and explains the reason rather than just refusing: the skill is shareable and version-controlled, sizes go stale as children grow, and a stale hardcoded size is worse than no size because it will be trusted. Offers the right home instead — the personal-records store (patching the measurement, not the size) or a local project file outside the skill directory. If a genuine method lesson came out of the run, offers to write that lesson into the skill with the personal specifics left out.

evals.prompt: Find my wife a winter coat from Aritzia — we haven't used that site before.
evals.expected_output: Reads references/retailer-recipes.md first, finds no recipe for this retailer, and works out the extraction method live — how to read title, price, per-size availability, and image. Then writes a new retailer section into the recipes file as part of the same run, without being asked: the country and segment it serves, the working snippet, a date-stamped selector table, and the failure modes hit along the way including any dead ends. Captures the selectors while the tab is still open rather than reconstructing them afterwards. Promotes anything that turned out to be true of all sites to the shared rules section instead of duplicating it. Adds no personal data — the recipe describes the site, never the wearer or her size. Mentions in the final report what was added to the skill and why.

evals.prompt: That Gap size-availability selector you have documented doesn't work anymore — the page markup changed.
evals.expected_output: Treats the stale recipe as a bug in the skill, not just an obstacle in the run: re-derives the working selector from the live page, then corrects the existing entry in references/retailer-recipes.md rather than appending a second contradictory note beside it. Re-stamps the verification date so a future reader knows which is current. Does not silently keep browsing with the new selector and leave the file wrong, since a stale recipe is worse than a missing one — it gets trusted. Says what changed in the report.
